title: Vault Fork OpenBao Adds External Keys and Quantum-Ready TLS
gist: OpenBao 2.7, the Linux Foundation-governed MPL fork of HashiCorp Vault, adds PostgreSQL read scaling, external HSM/KMS-backed keys, ML-DSA/ML-KEM post-quantum algorithms and control groups, offering open versions of features Vault kept behind enterprise licences. With commercial support from ControlPlane and plugin-based restructuring, the author sees the fork becoming a credible Vault alternative rather than a protest project.

insights.claim: OpenBao began as a community fork of HashiCorp Vault after HashiCorp moved Vault from the Mozilla Public License to the Business Source License in 2023, and is now governed under the Linux Foundation's Open Source Security Foundation under MPL 2.0.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Licence changes by infrastructure vendors can spawn foundation-backed competitors that erode pricing power.
insights.locator: OpenBao began as a community fork

insights.claim: The OpenBao fork was both ideological and commercial: Vault had placed namespaces, HSM integration and advanced scalability behind enterprise licences, which an open fork could offer without restriction, following the pattern that produced OpenTofu from Terraform and Valkey from Redis.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Open-core vendors that gate key features face forks that commoditize their enterprise tiers.
insights.quote: The fork was both ideological and commercial.
insights.locator: The fork was both ideological and

insights.claim: OpenBao's progress, including namespaces, plugin-based auto-unseal and Raft read scaling added since the fork, suggests it is becoming a credible alternative to Vault rather than merely a protest project.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Competitive risk to IBM's HashiCorp Vault enterprise revenue.
insights.quote: the fork is becoming a credible alternative rather than merely a protest project.
insights.locator: Secrets management being a foundational dependency

insights.claim: OpenBao 2.7 extends read scaling to PostgreSQL-backed deployments so standby instances can serve reads, similar to its Raft backend.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Horizontal scale removes a reason enterprises paid for Vault Enterprise.
insights.locator: OpenBao has developed well beyond a

insights.claim: OpenBao 2.7 lets PKI and Transit secrets engines use key material held in an external HSM or KMS via third-party plugins, letting operators run a PKI root backed by an HSM comparable to Vault Enterprise managed keys.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Directly matches a Vault Enterprise paid feature, weakening its upsell.
insights.quote: run your PKI root backed by an HSM

insights.claim: OpenBao 2.7 adds ML-DSA and ML-KEM to TLS listeners, certificate authentication, PKI and Transit, though a deployment is not quantum-safe unless clients, certificate authorities and surrounding systems also support the algorithms.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Post-quantum migration is becoming a real product requirement across security infrastructure.
insights.quote: The change does not by itself make a deployment quantum-safe

insights.claim: Post-quantum support matters ahead of government transitions expected around 2030 because encrypted traffic recorded today could be decrypted in the future.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Harvest-now-decrypt-later risk sets a ~2030 deadline driving PQC spending.

insights.claim: OpenBao control groups add a control_group stanza to ACL policies requiring a second party to approve access to specified high-risk paths.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Another enterprise-style governance feature made available for free.
insights.locator: Control groups add an approval workflow

insights.claim: OpenBao 2.7 includes breaking changes: the HSM distribution is discontinued as PKCS#11 is externalized, cloud auto-unseal for Alibaba Cloud, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud moved to plugins, several auth methods moved to openbao-plugins, and the file storage backend was removed.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Plugin lifecycle management becomes a migration cost for adopters.
insights.locator: The release also includes breaking changes

insights.claim: ControlPlane launched ControlPlane Enterprise for OpenBao in March, offering security hardening, supply-chain assurance, rapid CVE remediation, optional FIPS 140-3 compliance support and 24/7 support, while noting OpenBao retains API compatibility with Vault for many use cases.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Third-party support vendors make the fork viable for regulated enterprises, accelerating Vault displacement.
insights.locator: Commercial support is also becoming part

insights.claim: Freely licensed open-source projects can sustain commercial ecosystems in which vendors compete on operational assurance rather than licence control.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Supports a services-and-assurance business model over source-available licensing.
insights.quote: an open-source project can remain freely licensed while vendors compete on operational assurance
insights.locator: Commercial support is also becoming part

insights.claim: For teams evaluating migration to OpenBao, the key questions are operational maturity, including plugin lifecycle management, PostgreSQL high availability, post-quantum client compatibility and production incident support, while version 2.8 is expected to focus on security, stability and authentication.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Operational maturity, not features, now gates OpenBao enterprise adoption.
